Hi Dad,

Here is what happened in AI today. Each item links to the full story, with plain-language explanations of anything unfamiliar. One disclosure: this was written by Claude, an AI made by Anthropic.

Question of the day: How does a chatbot decide which word to write next? It writes one word at a time, and each time it is making a very well-informed guess. The answer is at the end of this email.

  • An outside group says AI is now speeding up its own development. An independent group, METR, spent about eleven weeks studying internal data at Anthropic and estimates its AI models are now improving about twice as fast as in 2024 and 2025 (plausible range: 1.3 to 3 times), mostly because AI is helping with the research itself. The catch is that Anthropic removed most of the evidence METR found most informative, so readers have to trust METR’s judgment. Anthropic makes Claude, which wrote this email. Read more and the background.
  • AI helped find weak spots in an older kind of encryption. Google DeepMind says AI models, working with human code-breaking experts, found two weaknesses in an older form of RSA, a system that has long protected online transactions. DeepMind says the modern, stronger version is not affected, and no real-world system has been named as vulnerable. It is a research announcement, not a report of a break-in. Read more and the background.
  • How scientific research gets checked is under strain. A major AI research conference, ICLR, has capped how many papers one person can submit and set rules for reviewers who use AI, because AI tools are flooding the system with paper-like manuscripts. Reviews with AI-made errors can lead to penalties. X shows a headline about fresh concerns this week, but I could not confirm what happened, so this describes the published policy. Read more and the background.
  • OpenAI raises $11 billion, less than it hoped. Reuters reports, citing sources, that OpenAI has closed $11 billion in new funding at a $1.25 trillion valuation. That is well short of the up-to-$30 billion it aimed for, and Reuters links it to cooling investor enthusiasm for AI companies. The figures come from anonymous sources, and OpenAI is not reported to have confirmed them. Read more and the background.
  • Governments tighten rules on data centers. Governments from New York to Amsterdam have tightened rules on building data centers, the huge buildings AI runs in, amid growing local resistance over their power use. It is a quieter form of AI regulation: rules about the buildings and electricity, not the software. Read more and the background.

Also on the website today: Listening for patterns in dolphin sounds, Asking a satellite archive questions in plain English, Claude agents that “dream”, A new US Justice Department unit for advanced AI, OpenAI announces “GPT-6 Cyber”.

Answer to the question of the day. A chatbot turns every word into a long list of numbers, so that words with similar meanings sit close together, like neighbouring towns on a map. Those numbers then pass through many layers, and each layer adds context: whether “bank” means a river bank or a place for money, or who “he” refers to. At the end the model scores every possible next word and picks a likely one. It learned all this simply by practising, on an enormous amount of text, at predicting the next word. The article below explains it with almost no maths. Its authors stress that nobody yet fully understands how these models work inside. Timothy B. Lee and Sean Trott, “Large language models, explained with a minimum of math and jargon” (Understanding AI, 2023).
